incident_spec.summary: A single-row insert into a heavily indexed, large table sometimes stalls for minutes; the strongest evidence points to lock blocking from an idle or sleeping transaction, not table size alone.
symptoms: A simple insert sometimes takes over 7 minutes.
The insert blocks other activity and appears to stall the system.
dm_exec_requests reports a blocking session id that does not appear as an active request.
The blocker session still exists in dm_exec_sessions and is sleeping.
Blocked requests report wait type LCK_M_S.
incident_spec.mechanism: A long-lived open transaction holds a lock on the hot insert key or key range, so the insert waits behind that lock. The SQL Server-specific DMV mismatch is consistent with the blocker being an idle session that still owns locks rather than an actively running request. The many extra indexes may add normal write cost, but they do not explain a multi-minute outlier as well as blocking does.

facts.evidence: “The table is something like 8 million rows”
“although this particular table does have a Clustered Index, it has 34 other indexes”
“There are no triggers that I can see”
“The following simple insert took over 7 minutes”
The post describes a blocker id in dm_exec_requests that is absent from the requests DMV but present and sleeping in dm_exec_sessions.
“the blocked requests ... was waiting for a LCK_M_S”

value.likely_cause: blocking rather than raw insert cost

facts.evidence: Accepted answer argues the insert was likely blocked for most of its runtime.

assumptions: The slow insert is caused by a lock wait on the inserted key or range, not by CPU, I/O, or pure index maintenance alone.
comm_channelid = 11 is the hot value involved in the blocked path.
A MySQL InnoDB next-key or record lock can be used as a mechanism-level stand-in for the SQL Server blocking symptom.
unknowns: The exact blocking SQL statement and isolation level are not known.
The exact SQL Server lock mode and object involved in production are not known.
It is unknown whether the blocker is an orphaned connection, an idle transaction, or another application bug.
The precise definitions of the 34 indexes are not available.

feasibility.rationale: The available executor only supports MySQL, so the SQL Server-specific DMV behavior and LCK_M_S naming cannot be reproduced exactly. A mechanism-level reproduction of the symptom is still feasible by holding a lock on a hot secondary-index key in MySQL and showing that the insert blocks until the sleeping transaction commits.
missing_capabilities: SQL Server DMV visibility for sys.dm_exec_requests/sys.dm_exec_sessions
unmatched_conditions: Cannot reproduce the exact dm_exec_requests blocker-missing artifact
Cannot reproduce the exact LCK_M_S wait label
Cannot claim exact production accident reproduction

tables.name: communication
tables.purpose: Primary synthetic table used to reproduce a blocked single-row insert against a hot key while also mirroring the heavy index maintenance burden described in the post.
tables.distribution_notes: Rows are mostly spread across comm_channelid values 100-499, with comm_channelid=11 forced into a hot 1% hotspot. The table is deliberately over-indexed with 34 secondary indexes to mirror the reported OLTP design, but the reproduced outlier should come from lock blocking, not raw index count.

value_skew.communication.comm_channelid: 11 is a deliberate hotspot at roughly 1% of rows; other values are broadly spread across 100-499
value_skew.communication.comm_action: Deskwork is more common than the other labels to keep the insert shape realistic

calibration_queries.sql: SELECT id, comm_action FROM communication WHERE comm_channelid = 11 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10
calibration_queries.objective: Verify that the hot key is visible as a narrow secondary-index access path and that the data shape is selective enough for a key-range lock to matter.
expected_evidence: The plan should use the comm_channelid access path rather than a broad table scan.
The plan should reflect a narrow predicate on the hot channel value.
The plan shape should be compatible with a lock-heavy hot key reproduction.

calibration_queries.sql: SELECT id, comm_action FROM communication WHERE comm_channelid = 101 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10
calibration_queries.objective: Provide a cold-key comparison that should remain selective and help distinguish a hotspot from the normal insert path.
expected_evidence: The plan should still be narrow and index-driven.
The comparison key should not be part of the artificial hotspot.
The result helps separate contention from ordinary write cost.

validation_criteria: A cold-key insert completes without waiting on a lock while the blocker is absent.
A hot-key insert blocks while the sleeping transaction remains open.
Committing the blocker releases the hot-key insert promptly.
The calibration EXPLAIN output continues to show the intended secondary-index access path, proving the data shape is appropriate for the lock-wait mechanism.
symptom_evidence: Blocked insert latency is a clear outlier versus the baseline insert.
The blocker can be idle or sleeping while still holding locks.
The wait is attributable to a transaction boundary, not to a trigger or DDL event.
mechanism_evidence: The insert on comm_channelid = 11 waits until the lock-holding transaction commits.
The same statement on a cold key does not reproduce the delay.
The hotspot is driven by lock ownership on a secondary index key range.

experiment_request.dba_description: Reproduce a blocked single-row insert against a hot key in a heavily indexed table so the test can distinguish blocking from ordinary insert overhead.

unresolved_critical_questions: Was the production blocker an idle transaction, a long-running read, or another writer?
Which SQL Server lock mode actually held the insert up?
Do any of the 34 indexes participate in the real contention path, or are they only amplifying the normal write cost?
rationale: The post strongly indicates blocking, not simply a slow insert caused by table size or index count. Because the executor only supports MySQL, the plan uses a dedicated MySQL database with an over-indexed communication table and a sleeping transaction that holds a hot secondary-index lock. That reproduces the mechanism-level symptom of a single insert stalling behind an apparently idle blocker, while explicitly not claiming exact SQL Server DMV reproduction.
